name: Aspirin mask

angle.text: Users crush aspirin into a paste and apply it to the face for acne and redness, reasoning from aspirin's relation to salicylic acid. Salicylic acid itself is studied for acne; the aspirin mask has not been.

summary: Crushed-aspirin face paste for acne; relies on its link to salicylic acid, with no studies found.
note: Oral aspirin has documented warnings; topical mask effects are not described in sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
People crush aspirin tablets into a paste and apply it to the face for acne.
The idea rests on aspirin's relation to salicylic acid; no studies of the mask were found.
How it works: Aspirin converts to salicylic acid in the body; believers expect a similar anti-acne effect topically, which is untested.
Risks and caveats: Documented warnings concern oral aspirin; topical risks are not described in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
An aspirin mask is a home paste made by crushing aspirin tablets, applied to the face, mainly for acne and redness. Proponents note that aspirin is related to salicylic acid, a common acne ingredient.
Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid and is broken down in the body to salicylic acid . Wikipedia's aspirin article does not discuss acne use, and no studies of aspirin masks were found.

name: Honey mask (manuka)

angle.text: Skincare fans apply manuka honey as a mask to calm skin and clear breakouts. Honey has been studied in wound care, but no acne studies were found.

summary: Manuka honey smeared on the face for acne; wound studies exist for honey, but none for acne were found.
note: Authenticity and grading of manuka products are disputed.
currentQuick:
People apply manuka honey as a face mask to calm acne and skin.
Honey has some wound-care evidence, but no acne studies were found.
How it works: Proponents attribute effects to methylglyoxal and antibacterial activity seen in lab studies; effects on acne are untested.
Risks and caveats: Honey is generally safe in food amounts; labelling and authenticity of manuka honey are disputed. Honey is advised against for babies.
deepLead:
A manuka honey mask is honey from the mānuka tree applied to the face, used by proponents for acne and skin calming.
Mānuka honey is made from the nectar of Leptospermum scoparium, native to New Zealand and coastal Australia; its activity is attributed in part to methylglyoxal and graded by systems such as UMF and MGO . Honey in general shows antibacterial activity in laboratory studies and preliminary evidence of faster healing of partial-thickness burns . Neither page contains clinical evidence on acne.

name: Bentonite / clay mask

angle.text: People with oily or congested skin use wash-off bentonite clay masks to soak up oil for a less shiny, cleaner-looking face. The cosmetic claims rest on the clay's absorbency and common use; no clinical trials were found.

summary: Oil-absorbing clay paste for rinse-off masks; popular for oily skin but with no clinical trials behind the cosmetic claims.
note: No clinical trials of clay masks for oil control or acne were found.
currentQuick:
A bentonite mask is a wash-off paste made from an absorbent volcanic-ash clay. It is used in skincare routines for oily or congested skin.
The clay is a well-characterised industrial material, but no clinical studies of its cosmetic effect were found.
How it works: Bentonite particles are flat with a large surface area and swell in water, so they adsorb liquids and oils. Proponents attribute the mask's oil-absorbing effect to these properties; any effect is expected to last only until sebum returns.
Risks and caveats: Bentonite is described as meeting FDA standards for contact with food and drugs, though the FDA has warned about at least one retail bentonite clay product. Individual products and skin reactions vary.
deepLead:
A bentonite clay mask is a wash-off facial or body product whose main ingredient is bentonite, an absorbent clay composed mostly of the mineral montmorillonite. Such masks are marketed for soaking up skin oil and are used in skincare routines aimed at oily or congested skin .
Bentonite itself is an industrial and commercial material with many non-cosmetic uses, including drilling fluids, cat litter and wine clarification . No published human trial identified for this article has tested clay masks for oil control or acne, so claims about their cosmetic effects rest on the clay's known physical properties and on user reports rather than on clinical evidence.

name: Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) high dose

angle.text: Skincare and looksmaxxing posters take very high-dose vitamin B5 hoping to reduce skin oil and acne. The theory draws on its role in fatty acid metabolism; no acne trials were found.

summary: Megadose B5 pitched for oil control; no acne trials found, though no upper intake limit exists.
note: Acne and sebum claims are untested in the sources reviewed; users report their own breakouts.
currentQuick:
Vitamin B5 is an essential vitamin sold over the counter. Some people take very large amounts hoping to reduce sebum and acne.
No clinical studies of high-dose B5 for skin were found, and the reference sources do not discuss acne.
How it works: B5 is needed to make coenzyme A, which participates in fatty acid metabolism. Proponents reason that this link could affect sebum; this has not been tested in the studies identified here.
Risks and caveats: No tolerable upper intake level has been set because no harm from high doses has been documented in humans. Some community members describe breakouts of their own; no published studies were identified on this.
deepLead:
Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) is a water-soluble vitamin that animals need to make coenzyme A, which is involved in energy metabolism and fatty acid synthesis . In looksmaxxing and skincare circles, very high supplemental intakes are discussed as a way to reduce skin oil and acne.
The reference text consulted for this article does not mention acne, and no clinical studies of high-dose pantothenic acid for acne or sebum were identified. No upper intake limit has been set by US or European authorities, because no human evidence of harm from high doses has been found .

name: Probiotics for acne

angle.text: Acne-prone users take oral probiotics or use topical ones based on the gut-skin axis and the skin microbiome. Reviews and trials exist, but the evidence is preliminary and strain-specific.

summary: Gut-skin axis supplements and creams for acne; reviews and trials exist, but evidence is preliminary and strain-specific.
note: Benefits are strain-specific; higher infection risk in immunocompromised people.
currentQuick:
Probiotics are live bacteria sold as capsules, foods or skin products. For acne they are used on the idea that gut or skin microbes influence breakouts.
Several meta-analyses of randomised trials appeared in 2025, and reviews describe the evidence as preliminary.
How it works: Proposed routes are the gut-skin axis (gut microbes affecting inflammation and hormones) and shifts in skin bacteria such as C. acnes. A lab study found skin S. epidermidis can inhibit C. acnes via fermentation.
Risks and caveats: Probiotics are generally considered safe, but rare bloodstream infections have occurred in immunocompromised or critically ill people. Effects are strain-specific, and regulators such as EFSA have rejected probiotic health claims for insufficient evidence.
deepLead:
Probiotics are live microorganisms intended to confer a health benefit, sold as supplements, in fermented foods and in some topical products . For acne, oral and topical probiotics are discussed on the basis of the proposed gut-skin axis and of the skin's own microbial community .
Published reviews describe the research as preliminary. A review summarised in Wikipedia describes probiotics and synbiotics as showing early potential to reduce inflammatory acne lesions and improve skin barrier function . Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised trials of oral probiotics were published in 2025 . Benefits of probiotics are generally strain-specific, so results do not transfer between products .

name: DIM supplement

angle.text: Used off-label for hormonal acne, DIM is taken by users who want to change estrogen and androgen balance for clearer skin. The research on DIM concerns hormones and cancer; acne has not been studied.

summary: Broccoli-derived estrogen-metabolism supplement used for hormonal acne; the research is on cancer and hormones, not skin.
note: No acne or appearance trials found; human studies cover other conditions.
currentQuick:
DIM is a compound made from cruciferous vegetables and sold as a supplement. In acne communities it is used with the idea that it shifts estrogen metabolism and calms hormonal breakouts.
No clinical studies of DIM for acne were found; human research has focused on cancer and other conditions.
How it works: DIM forms from indole-3-carbinol in the stomach. Lab studies report antiestrogenic activity via the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and altered sex hormone metabolism.
Risks and caveats: Pure DIM carries skin, eye and respiratory irritation hazard labelling. Long-term effects of supplementation for acne have not been studied in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
3,3'-Diindolylmethane (DIM) is a compound formed when the body digests indole-3-carbinol, which occurs in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage and Brussels sprouts. It is sold as a dietary supplement .
In looksmaxxing and acne circles, DIM is promoted as an estrogen-metabolism supplement for hormonal acne. The research identified for this article concerns cancer chemoprevention, hormone metabolism and laboratory biology; no clinical studies of DIM for acne or appearance were found.

name: Hypochlorous acid spray

angle.text: Acne-prone users mist hypochlorous acid on face or body to reduce bacteria and soothe irritation. It is established in wound and eyelid care; its appearance use for acne has not been tested.

summary: Mist version of a chemical your white blood cells make; established in wound and eyelid care, untested for looks.
note: Short shelf life; no appearance trials found.
currentQuick:
A hypochlorous acid spray is a mild antimicrobial mist used on skin. HOCl is the same chemical neutrophils make to kill microbes.
It has regulatory clearance and studies in wound and eyelid care, but none specific to cosmetic outcomes were found.
How it works: HOCl oxidises microbial proteins and damages membranes. In one study, an HOCl eyelid solution cut staphylococci by over 99% in 20 minutes.
Risks and caveats: The EPA classes it as non-hazardous, though as an oxidiser it can irritate depending on concentration. Solutions degrade and lose potency with time, heat and light.
deepLead:
Hypochlorous acid (HOCl) spray is a mist containing a dilute solution of hypochlorous acid, a weak acid that forms when chlorine dissolves in water. It is marketed as a skin-safe antimicrobial for face and body care .
HOCl is also made naturally by neutrophils, which use it to kill microbes . Since 2016 the US FDA has cleared products with HOCl as the main active ingredient for treating wounds and infections, and it is approved as a saline preservative . No clinical studies of HOCl sprays for cosmetic appearance outcomes such as acne were identified.

name: Accure laser (1726 nm)

angle.text: Accure is an in-office 1726 nm laser used to shrink the oil glands behind persistent acne, similar to Aviclear. Registered trials exist, but published results were not found in the sources reviewed.

summary: 1726 nm laser aimed at oil glands for acne; registered trials exist but published results were not found here.
note: Results of registered trials were not available in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Accure is a clinic laser using a 1726 nm wavelength to target sebaceous glands in acne.
Trial registrations exist for similar devices, but the registry entries do not report outcomes.
How it works: The wavelength is described as selective for sebaceous glands, aiming to reduce oil production rather than act on the whole skin surface.
Risks and caveats: Side effects were not reported in the sources reviewed. Cost and availability vary by clinic.
deepLead:
Accure is a laser procedure that targets sebaceous (oil) glands with a 1726 nm wavelength as a treatment for acne. It belongs to the same class of selective sebaceous-gland lasers as Aviclear .
Source material for this article is limited to trial registrations. They show a completed 104-participant device study for acne  and a 30-participant laser study for acne . Outcomes are not reported in the registry entries.

name: Isolaz / pulsed light acne treatment

chain: Vacuum clears pores, light hits bacteria
angle.text: Isolaz is a clinic treatment combining suction and pulsed light, discussed in looksmaxxing circles for clogged pores and acne-prone skin. Public evidence behind it is thin.

summary: Vacuum plus pulsed light for clogged pores; a clinic add-on with thin public evidence behind it.
note: Light therapies are generally adjuncts; darker skin tones carry pigmentation risk with IPL.
currentQuick:
Isolaz-style treatments pair suction on the skin with pulses of broad-spectrum light, and are offered in clinics for acne and congested pores.
General acne references describe light therapies as add-on options with limited evidence rather than first-line care.
How it works: IPL light is absorbed by pigment, blood and water in the skin; the vacuum component is said by proponents to help clear pores.
Risks and caveats: Reported IPL complications include hyperpigmentation, and certain medications and skin conditions are contraindications. Results depend on skin tone and the practitioner.
deepLead:
Isolaz is a brand of in-office device that combines suction (vacuum) applied to the skin with pulses of broad-spectrum light, marketed for clogged pores and acne. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed under the broader heading of pulsed-light treatments for acne-prone skin.
Intense pulsed light (IPL) is a technology that uses a flashlamp to emit light of roughly 400 to 1200 nm, filtered to exclude ultraviolet and long infrared wavelengths. Acne is among the conditions for which IPL is used, alongside hair removal, pigmentation and vascular lesions . A general acne reference states that light and laser therapies are not first-line acne treatments and are usually used as add-ons because of cost and limited evidence .
Published information on the vacuum-assisted device specifically is thin, and this article is therefore short.

name: Sun exposure for acne

angle.text: Some people sit in the sun or tan hoping to dry out blemishes, and report short-term improvement in how skin looks. Reference sources link sun exposure to lingering dark marks rather than clearer skin.

summary: Tanning to dry out spots; reference sources link sun to lingering dark marks rather than clearer skin.
note: Sun can prolong post-acne pigmentation per general references.
currentQuick:
Some people tan or sunbathe in the hope of drying out acne. The effect, when reported, is described as temporary.
General references say sunlight is not associated with acne overall but can sustain post-acne dark marks.
How it works: Proponents say UV makes blemishes look drier and less red; no published trial supports it as a treatment.
Risks and caveats: UV can sustain postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, and intense UVA can trigger acne aestivalis; sunscreen is advised by references.
deepLead:
Sun exposure for acne is the practice of tanning or sitting in sunlight in the belief that it dries out blemishes. Community members sometimes report a short-term improvement in appearance.
General acne references state that sunlight exposure is not associated with acne overall, that intense UVA can trigger a separate eruption called acne aestivalis, and that sun exposure can prolong postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, for which daily sunscreen is advised . A study of acne patients also examined the link between postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and melasma .

name: Face-touching / phone hygiene habit

angle.text: Skincare communities suggest wiping phones, washing pillowcases and keeping hands off the face to cut down on breakouts and keep skin clearer. It is a low-effort routine, and its effect on acne has not been tested directly.

summary: Wiping phones and washing pillowcases to cut breakouts; untested, low-stakes routine.
currentQuick:
People wipe phones, change pillowcases and avoid touching their faces hoping to reduce breakouts.
No studies reviewed test these habits directly.
How it works: Proponents say it limits oil, dirt and friction against the skin; references note friction can aggravate existing acne.
Risks and caveats: No specific risks are documented; references also say over-washing is not recommended.
deepLead:
The face-touching and phone hygiene habit refers to wiping phones, washing pillowcases and avoiding touching the face in order to reduce breakouts. It is a lifestyle routine discussed in skincare circles.
General acne references report that cleanliness is not associated with acne, that washing affected skin more than twice daily is generally not recommended, and that mechanical pressure from helmets or chinstraps can worsen existing acne (acne mechanica) . They do not address phones or pillowcases specifically.

name: Minimalist routine (gentle cleanser + moisturizer)

angle.text: Users strip their routine to a gentle cleanser and moisturizer to avoid irritating the skin barrier, aiming for calmer, less breakout-prone skin. The approach is consistent with general dermatology guidance on the barrier, though the minimalist routine itself has not been trialled for acne.

summary: Gentle cleanser plus moisturizer; consistent with general dermatology guidance on the barrier.
currentQuick:
A pared-back routine using a gentle cleanser and moisturizer, aimed at avoiding barrier irritation.
General acne references recommend moisturizing and limiting washing frequency.
How it works: Reducing harsh products and supporting the barrier with moisturizer.
Risks and caveats: No specific risks documented; it does not itself treat acne.
deepLead:
A minimalist routine strips skincare down to a gentle cleanser and a moisturizer, often to avoid damaging the skin barrier with harsher products.
Wikipedia reports that dermatologists recommend non-comedogenic, oil-free products, that washing more than twice daily is generally discouraged, and that people with acne, even oily skin, should moisturize because barrier dysfunction may contribute to acne. A fragrance-free moisturizer may reduce irritation, and in one cited study a ceramide cleanser and cream were well tolerated alongside acne medication and improved adherence .

name: Silicone / onion extract scar gel (Mederma)

angle.text: Mederma and silicone gels or sheets are used to make scars look softer and less noticeable, including acne and surgical scars. Silicone products have a body of scar research behind them, while trials of the onion extract gel found results similar to petrolatum.

summary: OTC onion extract scar gel; trials found it no better than petrolatum.
note: Silicone products have somewhat more support than onion extract.
currentQuick:
Mederma is a popular OTC scar gel built around onion extract. Silicone gels and sheets are similar products.
Trials have generally not found it better than petrolatum.
How it works: Claimed to soften scars; a rabbit study found improved collagen organization without significant size reduction.
Risks and caveats: Safety data are limited in the sources reviewed; the product contains alcohol and fragrance.
deepLead:
Mederma is an over-the-counter gel marketed to make scars look softer and less noticeable; its name-giving ingredient is onion bulb extract, and the listed active ingredient is allantoin . Silicone gels and sheets are a related class of topical scar products.
Studies have mostly not favored Mederma over basic treatments. Two trials found onion extract gel no better than petrolatum, and a rabbit ear study found no significant reduction in scar size, height or inflammation .

name: Subcision

angle.text: Subcision is a clinic procedure used to lift rolling acne scars by releasing the fibrous bands pulling them down, giving a smoother surface. Evidence consists mostly of small studies, and forum claims that it beats other scar treatments or can be done at home are anecdotal.

summary: Needle release of tethered rolling scars; a recognized clinic procedure with mostly small-study evidence.
note: Described in medical sources as clinician-performed; DIY guides circulate online.
currentQuick:
Subcision uses a needle under the skin to cut the bands holding down depressed, rolling scars so they can lift.
It appears in dermatology reviews as part of multimodal scar treatment and is studied in small trials.
How it works: Releasing tethering fibres and creating a pocket where blood collects and collagen forms, which raises the scar.
Risks and caveats: Procedure-specific risks are not detailed in the sources reviewed; forum DIY versions are discussed online while medical sources describe it as in-office.
deepLead:
Subcision is a minor procedure in which a needle is inserted beneath the skin to release fibrous bands tethering a depressed scar, most often rolling acne scars. The term was coined in a 1995 paper describing a tri-beveled hypodermic needle introduced through a puncture .
Proponents say releasing the scar lets the skin rise and stimulates collagen. Studies include case series and small trials, and general reviews list it within multimodal acne scar treatment .

name: TCA CROSS

chain: Skin rebuilds collagen in the pit
angle.text: TCA CROSS is used by dermatologists to improve narrow, deep icepick acne scars by applying strong acid to individual scars. Small trials report improvement, including in darker skin types, with no large controlled studies.

summary: Dermatologist-applied pinpoint dabs of high-strength acid into icepick scars; small trials report improvement, with no large controlled evidence.
note: Trials are small and mostly open-label; the procedure is clinician-performed.
currentQuick:
TCA CROSS (chemical reconstruction of skin scars) is a dermatology procedure in which a clinician applies a high concentration of trichloroacetic acid to the base of individual atrophic acne scars, most often narrow icepick scars, rather than peeling the whole face.
Published studies, mostly small and many without a control group, report meaningful improvement in scar appearance after a series of sessions. Head-to-head trials against subcision, microneedling and pinpoint CO2 laser have produced mixed comparisons.
How it works: The acid is applied focally to the depressed scar and is thought to cause a controlled injury in the dermis, which authors propose triggers new collagen formation and lifts the scar floor. Studies describe this as dermal thickening rather than resurfacing of the surrounding skin.
Risks and caveats: The original authors reported no significant complications in a 65-patient series. Concentrations used in studies range from 50% to 100%; it is a clinician-performed procedure and acid at these strengths is not an over-the-counter product.
deepLead:
TCA CROSS, short for chemical reconstruction of skin scars, is a dermatologic technique for atrophic (depressed) acne scars in which a clinician applies a high-concentration trichloroacetic acid (TCA) solution to individual scars rather than to the whole face. It was described by Korean authors in a 2002 report on patients with dark skin types .
It is most associated with icepick scars and deep, narrow boxcar scars, which are described in dermatology literature as hard to improve with whole-face resurfacing . Published studies use concentrations from 50% to 100% and typically repeat sessions every few weeks .
The evidence consists mostly of small prospective or retrospective series, with a few randomised comparisons against other scar treatments. A 2017 systematic review examined the efficacy and adverse reactions of non-energy-based acne scar treatments . Review authors have noted that few randomised trials exist to identify any single gold-standard approach to acne scarring.

name: Punch excision / punch elevation

chain: Deep scar cut out or lifted
angle.text: Punch excision and elevation are used on deep boxcar acne scars, either removing the scar or raising its base to skin level. The techniques are long established in dermatology, with limited trial-level data.

summary: Surgical removal or lifting of individual deep acne scars with a small punch tool; long established in dermatology, with limited trial-level data.
note: A surgical procedure performed by clinicians; scarring from the procedure itself is a recognised possibility.
currentQuick:
Punch excision and punch elevation are minor surgical techniques for atrophic acne scars. In punch excision, a small circular blade removes the scar and the wound is closed; in punch elevation, the scar base is cut free and raised level with the surrounding skin.
They appear in dermatology treatment algorithms for deep boxcar and some icepick scars, usually alongside resurfacing such as lasers. Randomised trials identifying a best method are limited.
How it works: The techniques mechanically replace a deep, sharp-edged scar with either a fine linear closure or a lifted, healed base. Reviews describe them as often followed by resurfacing to blend the treated area.
Risks and caveats: As surgical procedures they carry the general risks of skin surgery, including a residual or new scar, infection and pigment change. Reviews generally describe them as clinician-performed and as part of combined approaches.
deepLead:
Punch excision and punch elevation are minor surgical techniques used on atrophic acne scars, particularly deep boxcar scars with sharp edges. In punch excision, a circular punch instrument removes the scar tissue and the defect is closed; in punch elevation, the base of the scar is separated and raised to the level of the surrounding skin .
Both were named in a widely cited 2001 review that proposed the icepick, rolling and boxcar classification of acne scars together with a treatment algorithm that also included subcision and laser resurfacing . A 2006 Swiss review likewise lists punch excision, punch elevation, subcision, dermal graft and fat transplantation as the surgical options, with dermabrasion or laser resurfacing as complements .
A 2024 narrative review notes that few randomised controlled trials have been designed to determine a gold-standard treatment for acne scars and that combining interventions would likely produce more benefit than a single method .

name: Phenol / Baker-Gordon peel

angle.text: The phenol or Baker-Gordon peel is the deepest classic chemical peel, used for coarse wrinkling, sun damage and some scarring to resurface the skin. It is performed under medical supervision, and its results are documented mainly in older clinical reports.

summary: The deepest classic chemical peel, a phenol and croton oil mixture with documented cardiac and pigment risks, performed under medical supervision.
note: Systemic absorption of phenol is reported to affect the heart; permanent lightening of skin is a reported effect.
currentQuick:
The Baker-Gordon peel is a deep chemical peel based on phenol and croton oil, introduced in the early 1960s. It is used to treat deep wrinkles, sun damage and some scarring, and is regarded in the medical literature as the strongest of the traditional peels.
Because of its depth, descriptions emphasise medical supervision, sedation or anaesthesia and monitoring, and a long recovery. In looksmaxxing discussions it is a rare, high-stakes procedure.
How it works: Phenol acts as a caustic, keratolytic agent that destroys the outer skin layers, and croton oil is described as the active ingredient that increases penetration. The injury is followed by skin regeneration over days to weeks.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include heart rhythm disturbances from systemic phenol absorption, permanent hypopigmentation, scarring, infection and herpes reactivation. Wikipedia notes that the deeper the peel, the more complications can arise. Descriptions of the procedure recommend cardiac monitoring and note it is generally limited to a single treatment per area.
deepLead:
The phenol or Baker-Gordon peel is a deep chemical peel in which a mixture containing phenol and croton oil is applied to the skin to produce a controlled deep injury, after which the skin regenerates. It is used for coarse wrinkling, sun-damaged skin and some scarring, and sits at the deepest end of chemical peeling .
Chemical peeling goes back to the second half of the nineteenth century, when Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra used phenol, croton oil and nitric acid for freckles and skin irregularities. Wikipedia states that phenol-croton oil peels were used discreetly by early Hollywood stars in the 1920s and entered mainstream practice in the 1960s through Thomas Baker and Howard Gordon . Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, gives 1961 for the Baker-Gordon formula .
Both sources describe the peel as carrying more risk than lighter peels, including cardiac and pigmentation effects . No clinical trials were located for this article; the information here comes from encyclopedic summaries, which themselves note limited sourcing.

name: PRP microneedling (vampire facial)

angle.text: The vampire facial pairs microneedling with a person's own platelet-rich plasma for skin rejuvenation and acne scarring. Microneedling itself is studied for scars, while the added benefit of PRP is considered unproven, and claims of quick scar clearance are anecdotal.

summary: Microneedling with a layer of your own platelet-rich plasma; popular and widely offered, but the added benefit of PRP is described as unproven, and unregulated spas have caused infections.
note: In 2024 the CDC reported HIV infections linked to an unlicensed spa offering vampire facials.
currentQuick:
PRP microneedling, marketed as the vampire facial, combines microneedling with platelet-rich plasma prepared from the client's own blood. It is offered for skin texture, acne scars and general rejuvenation, and gained attention through celebrity endorsement in the 2010s.
Studies of microneedling are mostly small, and Wikipedia describes the efficacy of adding PRP as in question pending scientific studies. On looksmax.org, users post before-and-after accounts and discuss DIY variants such as PRP creams.
How it works: Blood is drawn and spun in a centrifuge to concentrate platelets, which carry growth factors, and the plasma is applied during or after microneedling, which makes tiny punctures in the skin. Proponents say the growth factors boost healing and collagen production.
Risks and caveats: The main concern raised in sources is infection when procedures are done in non-medical settings with poor infection control. In April 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses among patients of an unlicensed Albuquerque spa; about 200 other clients and partners tested negative. PRP is exempt from FDA regulation as a product, while the preparation devices need clearance.
deepLead:
PRP microneedling, widely marketed as the vampire facial, is a cosmetic procedure that combines microneedling with platelet-rich plasma (PRP), a concentrate of a person's own blood plasma that is rich in platelets. It is offered for skin rejuvenation and acne scarring .
PRP is made by centrifuging a blood sample to remove most red cells while retaining platelets, which carry growth factors and cytokines; Wikipedia says the aim is to concentrate platelets to three to five times normal levels . Platelet concentrates differ in their preparation and are classified into several types in the literature . Wikipedia reports that vampire facials grew popular in the 2010s with celebrity endorsement and usually involve microneedling .
The evidence for PRP varies by use. A 2009 review described it as promising but not proven , and Wikipedia's microneedling article states that combining microneedling with PRP has efficacy in question pending scientific studies . Safety attention rose in April 2024, when the CDC reported HIV cases linked to a New Mexico spa .

name: Exosome treatments

angle.text: Exosome serums are applied after microneedling and marketed for rejuvenation, scars, under-eye concerns and hair. Exosome biology is well studied in labs, while cosmetic use on skin remains largely untested.

summary: Stem-cell-derived vesicle serums applied after microneedling; exosome biology is well studied, but cosmetic use is unproven and the FDA treats exosome products as drugs.
note: The FDA has stated exosome products are drugs requiring pre-market approval and has reported patient injuries linked to injections.
currentQuick:
Exosomes are tiny membrane-bound vesicles released by cells, and cosmetic products marketed as exosome serums use vesicles from sources such as stem cells, often applied after microneedling to skin said to be aging or scarred.
Laboratory research on exosomes is extensive, but clinical trials of cosmetic exosome products are few and small, and registered trials in skin aging and hair loss are early-stage or have ended without results being listed.
How it works: Exosomes carry proteins, lipids and nucleic acids between cells, and researchers study them as signalling carriers. Proponents of cosmetic use propose that these cargoes can signal skin cells to repair; whether functional transfer of this kind occurs in humans is described by Wikipedia as having limited definitive evidence.
Risks and caveats: In late 2019 the FDA issued an advisory about noncompliant exosome marketing and about patient injuries linked to exosome injections, stating that exosomes are drug products requiring pre-market approval. Wikipedia describes ongoing unapproved marketing of cosmetic exosome products. Products differ in source and purity.
deepLead:
Exosome treatments are cosmetic or medical-aesthetic products that use exosomes, small extracellular vesicles of roughly 30 to 150 nanometres released by cells, typically derived from stem cells and applied to the skin, frequently after microneedling . They are marketed for skin rejuvenation, scarring and hair.
Exosome biology is a major research field. A 2007 paper showed that exosomes from mast cells carry mRNAs and microRNAs that can be transferred between cells , and reviews describe exosomes as mediators of cell-to-cell communication . A position statement from the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles notes that the field uses many overlapping terms for vesicle types and sets minimal reporting standards .
Cosmetic use is far less studied. Registered trials of exosomes with microneedling for skin aging and for hair loss exist, but no published results were identified for this article . The FDA has said exosome products are drugs requiring pre-market approval .

name: Picosecond laser (PicoSure/PicoWay)

angle.text: Picosecond lasers are used in clinics for pigment, tattoos, texture and acne scars, aiming for smoother and more even skin. Small prospective studies report scar improvement, with few large trials.

summary: Ultra-short-pulse laser used for pigment, tattoos and acne scars; small prospective studies report scar improvement, with few large trials.
note: Clinic-performed; the main scar study was small, uncontrolled and limited to skin types III-IV.
currentQuick:
Picosecond lasers deliver energy in trillionths of a second. PicoSure and PicoWay are commercial devices of this type, used in clinics for tattoo and pigment treatment, skin texture and acne scars.
Published evidence for acne scars is limited to small prospective studies; a 2020 study of 18 completers reported improvement in scar grading scores after six sessions. Registered trials also cover wrinkles, melasma and skin tightening.
How it works: A fractionated picosecond laser creates tiny zones of injury in the epidermis. A microscopy study in one volunteer found micro-injuries concentrated in pigmented cells, with debris exfoliated over about four weeks, suggesting melanin as the main absorber of the beam.
Risks and caveats: The 2020 acne scar study concluded the treatment was safe in 18 patients with skin types III-IV, but no large safety dataset was identified, and pain was measured as an outcome. Results in other skin types are not covered. Treatments are performed in clinics.
deepLead:
Picosecond lasers are lasers whose pulses last a trillionth of a second, shorter than earlier nanosecond devices. PicoSure and PicoWay are among the commercial systems clinics use for pigmented lesions, tattoos, skin texture and acne scars. Registered trials cover tattoos, melasma, wrinkles, skin quality and facial laxity .
For acne scars, a 2020 prospective study of a fractionated dual-wavelength picosecond laser reported improvement in physician-rated scar scores and patient-rated scores; the authors said few prospective studies of this device in acne scars had been published . A 2017 imaging study described how fractionated non-ablative picosecond treatment injures skin on a microscopic level .
Evidence is small-scale: the studies identified here are one prospective study with 18 completers and one single-volunteer descriptive study.
